title: Reflux: the empirical trial, alarm features, and when to scope

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2022 ACG guideline on gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: For typical heartburn and regurgitation with no alarm features, how long is the empirical proton pump inhibitor trial?
questions.why: Once daily, 30 to 60 minutes before the first meal. Response supports the diagnosis; lack of response is a reason to look, not to double the dose indefinitely.

questions.q: Which alarm features mean endoscopy before, or instead of, an empirical trial?
a: Gastrointestinal bleeding or iron deficiency anaemia
questions.why: New symptoms after 60 are also on the list in many guidelines. Dysphagia in particular needs endoscopy to exclude a stricture, eosinophilic oesophagitis or cancer.

questions.q: When should a proton pump inhibitor be taken?
d: At bedtime on an empty stomach
Any time; timing does not matter
questions.why: The drug works on actively secreting pumps, which the meal switches on. Taking it at bedtime without food is the commonest reason for apparent failure.

questions.q: Symptoms have not improved after 8 weeks of a proton pump inhibitor taken correctly. What is next?
questions.a: Endoscopy, ideally off the drug for 2 to 4 weeks, with reflux monitoring if it is normal
d: Add an H2 blocker for a year
Diagnose functional heartburn and stop investigating
questions.why: Half of refractory patients do not have reflux at all. Objective evidence of reflux is required before any surgery or long-term escalation.

questions.q: Symptoms are controlled after the initial course. What happens to the proton pump inhibitor?
questions.a: Step down to the lowest effective dose, on-demand dosing, or an H2 blocker
d: Continue the full dose for life
questions.why: Rebound acid hypersecretion for a couple of weeks after stopping is expected and does not mean the drug is needed for ever. Erosive oesophagitis and Barrett's are the exceptions that stay on maintenance.

questions.q: Which associations with long-term proton pump inhibitor use have some evidence, enough to justify using the lowest effective dose?
questions.why: The associations are modest and mostly observational, and the guideline is clear that a needed drug is not stopped for them. It is the unneeded prescription that is the problem.

questions.q: Which risk factors, three or more of them with chronic reflux, prompt screening endoscopy for Barrett's oesophagus?
a: A first-degree relative with Barrett's or oesophageal adenocarcinoma
questions.why: Helicobacter pylori is, if anything, protective against Barrett's. Screening is a one-time endoscopy; if negative, it is not repeated.

questions.q: Which lifestyle measures have evidence in reflux?
a: Raising the head of the bed
Avoiding meals within 2 to 3 hours of lying down
questions.why: Left-side sleeping helps; the right side worsens reflux. Blanket food avoidance has little evidence; patients avoid what they notice triggers them.

questions.q: Chronic cough and hoarseness with no heartburn. What does the guideline advise about a proton pump inhibitor?
questions.a: Do not treat empirically long term; get objective reflux testing first
d: A high-dose PPI for a year
A PPI plus an H2 blocker
questions.why: Extra-oesophageal symptoms without typical reflux rarely respond to acid suppression. A short trial is reasonable only when typical symptoms are also present.

questions.q: A 30-year-old with intermittent food impaction and dysphagia. Which diagnosis must the endoscopist biopsy for?
questions.why: It is now the commonest cause of food bolus obstruction in young adults. Biopsies from several levels are needed because the changes are patchy.

questions.q: Chest pain that might be reflux in a 58-year-old with risk factors. What comes first?
questions.why: Reflux and coronary pain overlap, and both respond to nothing in particular in the moment. Only once the heart is cleared does the reflux pathway start.

questions.q: Who is a candidate for anti-reflux surgery?
questions.a: Proven reflux that responds to a PPI, in a patient who cannot or will not take it long term
d: Anyone with heartburn for more than a year
A patient whose symptoms did not respond to a PPI and whose testing was normal
questions.why: Non-response to a PPI with normal testing predicts a poor surgical result. Fundoplication and magnetic sphincter augmentation are the usual options.
